sections.title: Learning Objectives
items: Explain why polyprotic acids ionize stepwise and why each successive Ka is smaller
Perform equilibrium calculations for diprotic acids such as H2CO3 and H2S
Apply the 'moles first, react to completion, divide by total volume' method to mixed-solution problems
Predict which species dominate at each stage of a polyprotic titration
Combine acid-base equilibria with stoichiometry in multi-step calculations

sections.title: Concept 1 — Polyprotic Acids and Stepwise Ionization
body: A polyprotic acid has more than one ionizable proton. It ionizes in steps, one proton at a time: H2CO3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + HCO3−(aq) (Ka1 = 4.3 × 10−7), then HCO3−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + CO32−(aq) (Ka2 = 4.7 × 10−11).
Each successive ionization constant is smaller than the previous one — typically by a factor of 10^4–10^5 — because it is harder to remove a proton from a negatively charged ion.
Because Ka1 >> Ka2, the hydronium concentration in a solution of a diprotic acid is essentially determined by the first step alone. The second step contributes negligibly to [H3O+].
The intermediate ion (e.g., HCO3−, HSO4−) is amphiprotic: it can act as an acid (Ka2) or a base (Kb = Kw/Ka1).

worked_example.question: Calculate the concentration of H3O+ and the pH of a 0.050 M solution of H2S. Ka1 = 1.0 × 10−7, Ka2 = 1.0 × 10−19.
worked_example.solution: Use only Ka1: H2S + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + HS−. Ka1 = x²/(0.050 − x) ≈ x²/0.050 = 1.0 × 10−7 → x = √(5.0 × 10−9) = 7.1 × 10−5 M. pH = −log(7.1×10−5) = 4.15. (Ka2 is so small that the second step adds a negligible amount of H3O+.)

common_mistakes: Writing both ionization steps in one equation — polyprotic acids ionize one proton at a time.
Adding the H3O+ from the second step to the first step's result (negligible for typical problems).

sections.title: Concept 2 — Mixed-Solution Stoichiometry (the 'Moles First' Method)
body: When two solutions are mixed, the acid-base reaction is fast and goes to completion for strong acids/bases. Always: (1) convert to moles, (2) react to completion (find the limiting reactant and leftover), (3) divide by the TOTAL volume to get new concentrations, then (4) calculate pH from whatever remains.

If excess strong acid remains → pH from leftover [H3O+]. If excess strong base remains → pH from leftover [OH−]. If exactly neutralized with a weak partner → solve the hydrolysis (Kb or Ka) of the salt formed.
The total volume is the sum of both solution volumes — forgetting this is the most common error.

worked_example.question: 50.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.060 M NaOH. Find the pH of the resulting solution.
worked_example.solution: Moles HCl = 0.00500; moles NaOH = 0.00300. HCl is in excess by 0.00200 mol. Total volume = 0.100 L. [H3O+] = 0.00200/0.100 = 0.020 M. pH = −log(0.020) = 1.70.

common_mistakes: Using the original volumes instead of the total volume after mixing.
Neutralizing mole-for-mole without checking which reactant is in excess.

sections.title: Concept 3 — Polyprotic Titrations and Species Distribution
body: The titration curve of a diprotic acid (e.g., H3PO4, H2CO3) shows two equivalence points and two buffer regions. Between equivalence points, the intermediate species (H2PO4−, HPO42−) buffers the solution.
At the first half-equivalence point, [H3PO4] = [H2PO4−] and pH = pKa1. At the second half-equivalence point, [H2PO4−] = [HPO42−] and pH = pKa2.
Which species dominates depends on pH: H3PO4 dominates below pKa1, H2PO4− dominates between pKa1 and pKa2, and HPO42− dominates above pKa2.

worked_example.question: For phosphoric acid (pKa1 = 2.15, pKa2 = 7.20, pKa3 = 12.35), which species dominates at (a) pH 1.0 (b) pH 5.0 (c) pH 9.0?
worked_example.solution: (a) H3PO4 (below pKa1) (b) H2PO4− (between pKa1 and pKa2) (c) HPO42− (between pKa2 and pKa3).

common_mistakes: Expecting a single equivalence point for a polyprotic acid.
Choosing an indicator that changes color at the wrong equivalence point.

items.q: Explain why Ka2 is always smaller than Ka1 for a polyprotic acid such as H2CO3.
items.answer: Removing a proton from a negatively charged ion (e.g., HCO3− → CO32−) requires more energy than removing one from a neutral molecule. Electrostatic attraction makes the remaining proton harder to remove.

items.q: Write the two stepwise ionization equations for H2CO3, labeling Ka1 and Ka2.
items.answer: H2CO3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + HCO3−(aq) (Ka1); HCO3−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + CO32−(aq) (Ka2)

items.q: Which species are present in appreciable concentration in a solution of H2CO3? Explain why CO32− is present in only trace amounts.
items.answer: H2CO3, HCO3−, H3O+, and OH−. CO32− is present only in trace amounts because Ka2 (4.7 × 10−11) is tiny — very little HCO3− ionizes further.

items.q: Calculate the H3O+ concentration and pH of a 0.010 M solution of H2S. Ka1 = 1.0 × 10−7, Ka2 = 1.0 × 10−19.
items.answer: x²/0.010 = 1.0 × 10−7 → x = 3.2 × 10−5 M; pH = 4.50. (Second step negligible.)

items.q: For phosphoric acid (pKa1 = 2.15, pKa2 = 7.20, pKa3 = 12.35), identify the dominant species at pH 1.0, pH 5.0, pH 9.0, and pH 13.0.
25.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl is mixed with 75.0 mL of 0.050 M NaOH. Calculate the pH of the mixture.
items.answer: Moles HCl = 0.00500; moles NaOH = 0.00375. Excess HCl = 0.00125 mol in 0.100 L → [H3O+] = 0.0125 M; pH = 1.90.

items.q: 40.0 mL of 0.150 M KOH is mixed with 60.0 mL of 0.080 M HCl. Calculate the pH of the mixture.
items.answer: Moles KOH = 0.00600; moles HCl = 0.00480. Excess KOH = 0.00120 mol in 0.100 L → [OH−] = 0.0120 M; pOH = 1.92; pH = 12.08.

items.q: 30.0 mL of 0.100 M H2SO4 (diprotic, both protons strong) is mixed with 70.0 mL of 0.050 M NaOH. Calculate the pH.
50.0 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH is mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Ka = 1.8 × 10−5. Is the mixture a buffer? Calculate its pH.
100.0 mL of 0.050 M HCN (Ka = 6.2 × 10−10) is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution.
